steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction and related work for a short demo paper on a guardrail tool that post-processes LLM inputs and outputs to catch unsafe behavior. Explain why LLMs are widely used, what risks they pose, how existing mitigations fall short, and what the tool does.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Rise and wide use of LLMs
- Unsafe behaviours: privacy leaks, bias
- Existing mitigations and their cost; post-processing guardrails
- Our tool: LLMGuard

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have become important because they perform remarkably on many NLP tasks, like text generation, translation, summarization, question-answering and sentiment analysis. To some extent LLMs work as a general-purpose language task solver, and the research paradigm has been moving towards using them. With models like PaLM, GPT-3 and GPT-4, LLMs are used more and more in domains like medicine, education, finance and entertainment.

Even though they are so successful, LLMs often behave in ways that make them unsafe in different enterprise settings. For example, the text can include confidential or personal information like telephone numbers, which leads to privacy leaks. There are also reports of bias in LLM responses, which raises ethical concerns about deploying them in applications. One study gives a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of different kinds of biases shown by recent LLMs, such as race, gender, ethnicity, age, etc. These risks raise concerns about what the growing use of LLMs means for different areas, from education to heritage to healthcare.

- Mitigations
  - alignment with human preferences, e.g. RLHF (safety + helpfulness objectives)
  - red flagging and rectifying undesirable behaviours
  - constant retraining needed -> prohibitive
  - post-processing guardrails on LLM outputs, validating user and LLM responses
- LLMGuard
  - library of detectors on user questions + LLM responses
  - flags PII, bias, toxicity, violence, blacklisted topics
  - demo on FLAN-T5 and GPT-2; architecture in Figure 1

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have become important because they perform remarkably on many NLP tasks, like text generation, translation, summarization, question-answering and sentiment analysis. To some extent LLMs work as a general-purpose language task solver, and the research paradigm has been moving towards using them. With models like PaLM, GPT-3 and GPT-4, LLMs are used more and more in domains like medicine, education, finance and entertainment.

Even though they are so successful, LLMs often behave in ways that make them unsafe in different enterprise settings. For example, the text can include confidential or personal information like telephone numbers, which leads to privacy leaks. There are also reports of bias in LLM responses, which raises ethical concerns about deploying them in applications. One study gives a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of different kinds of biases shown by recent LLMs, such as race, gender, ethnicity, age, etc. These risks raise concerns about what the growing use of LLMs means for different areas, from education to heritage to healthcare.

To deal with these risks, different techniques have been proposed to align LLMs with human preferences. One is RLHF, which finetunes the model on safety and helpfulness objectives. Another approach is about red flagging and fixing undesirable language behaviours. But these techniques need constant retraining, which makes them prohibitive in many cases. A promising line of methods uses post-processing to put guardrails directly on the LLM outputs. This makes sure they stay within specific parameters by validating user and LLM responses.

In this work we propose a tool, LLMGuard, which uses a library of detectors to post-process user questions and LLM responses. The detectors flag undesirable inputs and responses, such as Personal Identifiable Information (PII), bias, toxicity, violence and blacklisted topics. Finally we give a demo of LLMGuard working on two recent LLMs, FLAN-T5 and GPT-2, and show that our framework is effective. Figure 1 shows a high-level architecture of the tool.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have risen in importance due to their remarkable performance across various NLP tasks, including text generation, translation, summarization, question-answering, and sentiment analysis [1,2,3]. To some extent, LLMs serve as a general-purpose language task solver, and the research paradigm has been shifting towards using them [4]. With the advent of models such as PaLM [5], GPT-3 [6] and GPT-4 [7], LLMs have found increased use in domains such as medicine [8], education [9], finance and entertainment [10].

Despite their success, LLMs often exhibit behaviours that make them unsafe in various enterprise settings. For instance, the text can contain confidential or personal information, such as telephone numbers, leading to privacy leaks [11]. Instances of bias have also been reported in LLM responses, raising ethical concerns when deploying them in various applications [12]. [13] presents a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of different kinds of biases, such as race, gender, ethnicity, age, etc., exhibited by recent LLMs. Such risks raise concerns about the implications of the growing use of LLMs in areas ranging from education to heritage to healthcare [14].

To address them, various techniques have been proposed to align LLMs with human preferences, such as RLHF, which finetunes the model based on safety and helpfulness objectives [15]. Another approach focuses on red flagging and rectifying undesirable language behaviours [16]. However, such techniques require constant retraining, making them prohibitive in many cases. A promising line of methods instead pursues post-processing to apply guardrails directly to the LLM outputs, ensuring they stay within specific parameters by validating user and LLM responses.

In this work, we propose LLMGuard, a tool which employs a library of detectors to post-process user questions and LLM responses. These detectors flag undesirable inputs and responses such as Personal Identifiable Information (PII), bias, toxicity, violence, and blacklisted topics. Lastly, we demonstrate how LLMGuard works on two recent LLMs, FLAN-T5 and GPT-2 [17,18], and show the effectiveness of our framework. A high-level architecture of the tool is shown in Figure 1.
